CEST-detectable metabolite candidates: intervertebral disc

1 of 4 candidates clear the simulated with-vs-without contrast threshold (0.5%) at some field strength, by chemical exchange (downfield, +ppm) or by the relayed NOE (upfield, −ppm). 1 fall below it; 2 are unknown because no group had a verified reference rate, so nothing could be simulated. The threshold applies to our own simulation, never to a literature MTRasym.

Glycosaminoglycan (GAG) – disaccharide repeating unit (chondroitin sulfate / keratan sulfate) — CEST: ✓ detectable (both)

Concentration: 100.00 mM typical (70–130 mM (disaccharide units in nucleus pulposus tissue water))

Estimated concentration — no direct literature value found. Reasoning: Estimate based on measured fixed charge density (FCD) of human and bovine nucleus pulposus. Each GAG disaccharide (chondroitin sulfate) carries ~2 negative charges. Bovine NP FCD = 0.19 ± 0.039 mEq/g wet tissue (PMID:19757059). Human cervical NP FCD = 0.18 ± 0.1 mEq/g wet tissue (PMID:39892283). Converting: 0.19 mEq/g wet tissue = 0.19 mmol negative charges/g. At 2 charges/disaccharide → 0.095 mmol disaccharide/g wet tissue. NP water content ~80% of wet weight → ~0.8 mL water/g tissue. Concentration in tissue water = 0.095 / 0.0008 L ≈ 119 mM. Rounding to ~100 mM as a typical estimate for healthy NP.

Recommended field strength(s): 0.5 T, 1.5 T, 3 T, 5 T, 7 T

Robustness to input uncertainty: robust

Uncertainty corners:

  • Contrast over the uncertainty corners (Sugar ring C-H (aliphatic rNOE) [rnoe]: concentration 70-130 mM, kex fixed at 5 s−1 (single measurement, spread unknown); N-acetyl amide NH (GlcNAc/GalNAc) [amide]: concentration 70-130 mM, kex 15-158 s−1; Hydroxyl OH (C2, C3, C6 on GalNAcS/Gal/Glc) [hydroxyl]: concentration 70-130 mM, kex fixed at 600 s−1 (single measurement, spread unknown)) at the swept B1/Tsat: 0.5 T: 1.01-1.86%, 1.5 T: 0.63-3.99%, 3 T: 2.81-5.04%, 5 T: 5.34-9.37%, 7 T: 7.63-13.06%.
  • Threshold 0.5%. Detectable even at the low corner.

Frequency-collision analysis:

  • At 0.5 T: best group is rNOE (-3.5 ppm, 1.44%) but collides with semisolid MT (-2.4 ppm): 23.4 Hz separation vs 15937 Hz linewidth — complete blurring. At 1.5 T: best group is amide (+3.5 ppm, 2.62%) but collides with MT: 377 Hz vs 15947 Hz — complete blurring. At 3–7 T: the hydroxyl group (+0.82 ppm, 3.9–10.5%) dominates.
  • At 3 T: collides with lactate hydroxyl (+0.75 ppm): 9.6 Hz vs 223 Hz — severe blurring. At 5 T: 16.0 Hz separation still < 223 Hz linewidth. At 7 T: 22.4 Hz still < 223 Hz. The GAG and lactate hydroxyl pools are inseparable at all fields.
  • The rNOE pools at -3.5 ppm are inseparable from MT at low fields only.

Direct water saturation: At 0.5 T (B1=0.25 µT): direct_sat_bandwidth=10.6 Hz. The hydroxyl at +0.82 ppm = 17.4 Hz offset, only ~7 Hz from the water saturation edge — partial masking occurs. At 1.5 T (B1=0.5 µT): hydroxyl at +0.82 ppm = 52 Hz, direct_sat_bw=21.3 Hz — safe. At 3–7 T: offsets are 105–245 Hz, well outside the 32–64 Hz direct saturation bandwidth. The rNOE at -3.5 ppm is far from water at all fields. No masking at ≥1.5 T.

Ex vivo / in vivo exchange-rate caveat:

  • Hydroxyl kex=600 s⁻¹ borrowed from myo-inositol in human brain (PMID 20951217) — no IVD-specific measurement. A porcine IVD study (PMID 27670140) directly measured GAG hydroxyl exchange rate as k_sw = 9.2×10⁶ × 10⁻pH + 196.9 s⁻¹. At disc pH ~6.5–7.2 this gives k_sw ~350–1600 s⁻¹, meaning the simulated 600 s⁻¹ is plausible but uncertain and pH-dependent.
  • The rNOE groups use a class-level 5 s⁻¹ from phantom (PMID 25996515) — not tissue-specific. The amide kex is purely generic brain value and does not represent GAG N-acetyl NH exchange.

Optimized saturation sequence by field strength (derived from a Bloch-McConnell B1×Tsat sweep):

  • 0.5 T: B1=0.25 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) —
    recommended sequence: 1.436% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 1.5 T: B1=0.5 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) —
    recommended sequence: 2.621% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 3 T: B1=0.75 µT, Tsat=1000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — Hydroxyl exchange at kex ~600 s⁻¹ is in the intermediate-fast regime at 3 T. B1=0.75 µT (γB1=31.9 Hz) satisfies ω₁ ≈ kex / (2π) for near-optimal saturation efficiency. 1 s Tsat provides sufficient steady-state magnetization. This matches the clinically optimized gagCEST parameters at 3 T (PMID 27439061: best at 0.8 µT, 1.0 s). All four simulated hydroxyl contrast groups converge to a maximum at this combination.
    recommended sequence: 3.949% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 5 T: B1=1 µT, Tsat=1000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — At 5 T the same hydroxyl kex is effectively faster relative to the water T₂*; higher B1 (1.0 µT, γB1=42.6 Hz) is needed to maintain saturation efficiency. 1 s Tsat balances SNR and specific absorption rate. The hydroxyl contrast peaks at 7.4% at this optimum.
    recommended sequence: 7.417% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 7 T: B1=1.5 µT, Tsat=750 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — At 7 T the higher B0 requires stronger B1 (1.5 µT, γB1=63.9 Hz) to compete with the water T₂* broadening. The shorter Tsat=750 ms reduces SAR while maintaining steady-state. The hydroxyl contrast peaks at 10.5% — the highest of any field. The exchange regime is still intermediate-to-slow relative to the water linewidth.
    recommended sequence: 10.456% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied

B1/Tsat vs. extraction method (click for note + literature)

Note:

  • At 3–7 T the hydroxyl group at ~0.8 ppm requires Lorentzian difference or multi-pool Lorentzian fitting because MTRasym at ±0.8 ppm is contaminated by the broad NOE asymmetry from upfield pools and semisolid MT. The gagCEST clinical literature at 3 T (PMID 29748204, 25339437, 26583472) uses MTRasym at ±0.8–1.0 ppm and reports values consistent with this simulation's 3.9%.
  • For exchange-rate quantification the omega-plot method with multiple B1 powers was demonstrated in porcine IVD (PMID 27670140). AREX can remove T1/direct-saturation bias and is preferred at lower B1 where exchange is slower.

Potential clinical impact

GAG hydroxyl (-OH) protons, gagCEST ~1 ppm: 3 CEST/NOE application and 3 metabolite-change studies verified (1 human, 5 animal; 0 humans, 5 animals; 9 dropped by verification). GagCEST is the best-established CEST technique in IVD. Four human in vivo studies at 3T and one at 7T show gagCEST correlates with Pfirrmann grade, pain, and GAG content. GAG depletion is universally confirmed by biochemical assays in humans, dogs, mice, rats, and sheep (but not horses). Pooled evidence strongly supports gagCEST as a biomarker for disc degeneration.

Caveats / critique (8 points, 368 words) — Concentration of 100 mM for the disaccharide repeating unit in nucleus pulposus is reasonable. Published GAG concentrations in healthy NP are approximately 50–1…
  • Concentration of 100 mM for the disaccharide repeating unit in nucleus pulposus is reasonable. Published GAG concentrations in healthy NP are approximately 50–120 mg/mL wet weight; 100 mM at MW ~500 Da gives ~50 mg/mL, which is in range.
  • However, GAG concentration varies strongly with age, degeneration, and disc level (PMID 25970563 shows MTRasym drops from ~3% at age 20 to ~0% at age 50). The range 70–130 mM covers healthy conditions but not severely degenerated discs.
  • CRITICAL: The gagCEST literature (PMID 22253087, 29748204, 27439061) attributes the gagCEST signal to hydroxyl (-OH) protons at ~0.8–1.0 ppm, NOT to the N-acetyl amide at +3.5 ppm.
  • The amide pool simulated at +3.5 ppm with kex=65.5 s⁻¹ is a generic amide class value — the N-acetyl NH in GAG polysaccharides exchanges more slowly due to steric hindrance and is NOT the source of clinical gagCEST contrast. The hydroxyl group (+0.825 ppm, kex=600 s⁻¹) is correctly identified as the actual gagCEST source.
  • Disagree with the N-acetyl CH3 glycoNOE being placed at -3.5 ppm — the methyl group resonates at ~+2.0 ppm (offset ~-2.7 ppm from water) not -3.5 ppm. Sugar ring C-H rNOE at -3.5 ppm is a coarse approximation — actual ring C-H spans +3 to +5.5 ppm.
  • Agent 2's claim that hydroxyl signals 'merge into the water peak making them poorly CEST-visible' directly contradicts the entire gagCEST clinical literature. The in vivo gagCEST peak in human disc is observed at approximately +0.8–1.0 ppm (hydroxyl), confirmed by multiple 3 T studies (PMID 29748204, 27439061, 26583472).
  • The amide at +3.5 ppm simulated here is NOT detected in gagCEST of intervertebral disc. The hydroxyl shift of 0.825 ppm from phantom data (PMID 30230599) and human knee cartilage (PMID 21460030) is consistent with the in vivo disc literature. None of consequence. The carboxylate group is deprotonated at pH 7.4.
  • Sulfate groups do not carry exchangeable protons at physiological pH. no SAR or hardware ceiling is applied: the recommended B1/Tsat is the sweep optimum, and deliverability must be checked against the scanner's SAR monitor The gagCEST effect originates from hydroxyl (-OH) and N-acetyl (-NH) exchangeable protons on GAG. Each disaccharide has ~3 exchangeable hydroxyls + one amide NH per unit.

Lactate — CEST: ✗ not detectable

Concentration: 5.00 mM typical (2–10 mM) animal evidence only

Estimated concentration — no direct literature value found. Reasoning: PMID:6814195 reports highest lactate concentrations in central canine disc with high production rate in NP. Numerical modeling studies of human IVD (PMID:18374341, PMID:21970697, PMID:40979636) assume central NP lactate ~5-10 mM. PMID:10632449 shows bovine disc lactate production nearly doubles under low O2. I estimate ~5 mM as a typical central NP value.

Robustness to input uncertainty: no

Uncertainty corners: Contrast over the uncertainty corners (Hydroxyl OH (C2) [hydroxyl]: concentration 2-10 mM, kex fixed at 600 s−1 (single measurement, spread unknown)) at the swept B1/Tsat: 0.5 T: 0.01-0.02%, 1.5 T: 0.01-0.05%, 3 T: 0.02-0.11%, 5 T: 0.04-0.20%, 7 T: 0.05-0.27%. Threshold 0.5%.

Frequency-collision analysis: At all fields, the lactate hydroxyl (+0.75 ppm) is separated from GAG hydroxyl (+0.82 ppm) by only 1.6–22.4 Hz, far less than the combined exchange-broadened linewidth of ~223 Hz. These pools blur together completely. Any lactate CEST signal would be indistinguishable from the much larger GAG hydroxyl signal. At 0.5 T also collides with MT (67.1 Hz vs 16032 Hz). This makes specific lactate detection in disc impossible via simple asymmetry analysis.

Direct water saturation: At 0.5 T (B1=0.25 µT): direct_sat_bandwidth=10.6 Hz, lactate hydroxyl at +0.75 ppm = 16 Hz offset — only ~5 Hz from direct saturation edge, significant masking. At ≥1.5 T: lactate hydroxyl offset (48–224 Hz) is beyond the direct saturation bandwidth (21–64 Hz). Not a limiting factor at higher fields, but the contrast is too low anyway.

Ex vivo / in vivo exchange-rate caveat:

  • The kex = 600 s⁻¹ is borrowed from myo-inositol in human brain (PMID 20951217) — not measured in lactate and not measured in disc. The true lactate hydroxyl kex is pH-dependent: at pH 7.0–7.4 it is approximately 800–2000 s⁻¹ (faster), which would worsen the contrast even further by pushing the peak closer to water.
  • The reference table provides no kex range for this pool, so uncertainty corners only reflect concentration variation and even those show peak contrast of 0.27% at 7 T.

B1/Tsat vs. extraction method (click for note + literature)

Note: If lactate were detectable at higher concentrations, Lorentzian difference or multi-pool fitting would be essential because of the severe overlap with the GAG hydroxyl peak. The omega-plot method has been used for lactate hydroxyl exchange-rate quantification in muscle (PMID 35645392). At the sub-0.2% contrast levels simulated here, no extraction method can reliably separate lactate from noise.

No citations.

Potential clinical impact

Lactate is not a typical CEST target (hydroxyl at ~0.5 ppm, not commonly used for gagCEST; no specific lactate CEST in IVD reported): 0 CEST/NOE application and 1 metabolite-change studies verified (1 human, 0 animal; 44 humans, 0 animals; 2 dropped by verification). No CEST/NOE studies of lactate in IVD were found. However, lactate changes in IVD are well documented: levels of 2-6 mM measured biochemically in human discs, with altered distribution detected by 1H-MRS even at Pfirrmann grade 1. Lactate accumulation from glycolysis under hypoxia contributes to acidic pH implicated in discogenic pain.

Caveats / critique (8 points, 335 words) — 5 mM is a reasonable resting lactate concentration in intervertebral disc. NP cells are glycolytic and produce lactate; reported values range 2–10 mM.…
  • 5 mM is a reasonable resting lactate concentration in intervertebral disc. NP cells are glycolytic and produce lactate; reported values range 2–10 mM.
  • During degeneration or painful discs, lactate may rise to 15+ mM due to poor clearance, but even at the upper bound (10 mM) the simulated contrast at 7 T is only 0.27% — well below the 0.5% threshold. Agree that the only exchangeable proton is the hydroxyl OH (C2). Correctly classified as hydroxyl.
  • Agent 2's claim that this OH 'exchanges too fast for CEST detection' is too strong: lactate CEST has been detected in human calf muscle post-exercise at 3 T (PMID 35645392), but at much higher concentrations (~15–20 mM). At 5 mM in disc, Agent 2's conclusion that contrast is negligible is correct.
  • The carboxylate (pKa 3.9) is correctly identified as deprotonated at pH 7.4. No chemical errors. The lactate hydroxyl is reported at ~0.75 ppm (PMID 35645392), which was used in the simulation. No discrepancy. None. The CH3 at 1.3 ppm and methine CH at ~4.1 ppm are non-exchangeable. Correctly excluded.

Potential clinical impact

Not a CEST pool; measured by 23Na-MRI (direct detection of 23Na nucleus, not exchange-based): 0 CEST/NOE application and 3 metabolite-change studies verified (2 human, 1 animal; 30 humans, 12 animals; 1 dropped by verification). Sodium is not an exchangeable-proton CEST target. However, 23Na MRI is a well-established GAG surrogate via fixed charge density. Human 23Na-MRI studies (n=40 in vivo, n=30 ex vivo) show strong aTSC decrease with Pfirrmann/Thompson grade and back pain severity, correlating with biochemical GAG content (R=0.71). Robust biomarker for disc degeneration.

Chloride ion (Cl⁻) — CEST: ? unknown (not simulated)

Concentration: 150.00 mM typical (100–200 mM)

Estimated concentration — no direct literature value found. Reasoning: PMID:40651968 models IVD as a charged mixture with Na⁺ and Cl⁻ solutes. To maintain electroneutrality with the high Na⁺ concentration (~250 mM) and the fixed negative charges of GAG (FCD ~0.19 mEq/g → ~200 mM negative charges in water), the Cl⁻ concentration is lower than in plasma. The Donnan equilibrium predicts Cl⁻ ≈ Na⁺ − FCD/water. With Na⁺ ~270 mM and FCD equivalent ~200 mM negative charges, Cl⁻ ≈ 70-150 mM. I estimate ~150 mM as a typical value above 1 mM.

In vivo verification: ROI-differential CEST scan — Sagittal midline slab through lumbar spine (L3-S1), centred at L4/L5 disc level, covering intervertebral discs, vertebral bodies, spinal canal, and paraspinal muscles.

Why this scan: Comparing GAG CEST contrast across ROIs with vastly different known GAG concentrations (nucleus pulposus >> annulus fibrosus >> paraspinal muscle ≈ CSF) will discriminate real GAG-specific amide CEST at 3.5 ppm from background MT/NOE effects that are similar across these soft tissues at a given offset.

ROIWhere it is drawnRole
nucleus pulposus target tissueCentral hyperintense region of each lumbar intervertebral disc on T2-weighted localizer (avoiding the annulus), drawn on 2-3 consecutive sagittal slices through the disc midline.Target tissue with highest GAG concentration; expected to show strongest gagCEST effect.
annulus fibrosus target tissuePeripheral hypointense rim of each lumbar disc on T2-weighted localizer, drawn as an annular ROI excluding the nucleus, on the same sagittal slices.Sub-region of target tissue with intermediate GAG concentration, lower than nucleus pulposus.
paraspinal muscleErector spinae / multifidus muscle bulk posterior to the vertebral laminae, avoiding visible fat streaks, drawn on the same sagittal slices lateral to the spine.Comparison tissue with minimal GAG content; negative control for GAG-specific CEST.
cerebrospinal fluidHyperintense CSF space within the spinal canal (thecal sac) at the same disc levels, drawn carefully to avoid cord and nerve roots.Comparison tissue with negligibly low GAG; provides a reference baseline for non-specific saturation effects.
vertebral body marrowTrabecular bone marrow space within the L4 and L5 vertebral bodies, avoiding cortical bone edges and basivertebral vein, drawn on the same midline sagittal slices.Comparison tissue with fat-rich marrow; helps distinguish GAG effect from fatty marrow NOE contributions.

Scan protocol: 3 T, pulsed Gaussian train, B1=0.8 µT, 30 pulses × 30 ms (interpulse delay 3.33 ms, duty cycle 90%), total Tsat=1000 ms, TR=3500 ms

SAR reasoning (the experimentalist agent's own; the pipeline applies no SAR model): At 3 T, a 30-pulse train of 30 ms Gaussian pulses at B1=0.8 µT with 90% duty cycle delivers ~0.6 W/kg average RF power to the lumbar spine region, well within FDA/ICE limits for spine imaging. The long TR (3.5 s) allows full T1 recovery and SAR dissipation. Body coil transmission with vertebral body shielding further reduces local SAR hotspots.

Compromise rationale: The single metabolite (GAG) has one optimal saturation regime. The physicist's simulation at 3 T recommended B1=0.75 µT and Tsat=1000 ms. Our compromise at 0.8 µT, 1000 ms is nearly identical. This B1 favours the slow-intermediate amide NH exchange at 3.5 ppm while partially suppressing fast-exchanging hydroxyl pools at 0.8 ppm. The higher B1 (1.04 µT, +30%) still produces usable contrast within ±30% RF inhomogeneity, while lower B1 (0.56 µT) will reduce gagCEST by ~30% but remains detectable.

Fat suppression: SPAIR (Spectral Attenuated Inversion Recovery) fat-suppression prepulse applied before each readout train. Essential because vertebral body marrow and paraspinal fat produce strong MR signal at 3 T; unsuppressed fat would contaminate Z-spectra near 0 ppm and confound asymmetry analysis at both 3.5 and -3.5 ppm.

Motion mitigation: Respiratory bellows triggering with acceptance window in end-expiration (minimal diaphragm motion). Each Z-spectrum offset acquired within a single breath-hold (8-12 s) or with navigator-gated free-breathing for patients unable to hold breath. Scan time approximately 17 offsets × 3-4 averages × 3.5 s TR = 4-5 minutes per saturation power.

Slice coverage: Mid-sagittal 3-slice slab (thickness 5 mm each, gap 0.5 mm, total slab ~16.5 mm) centred at L4/L5 intervertebral disc level, extending from L3 mid-body to S1 upper endplate. This captures lumbar discs (L3/L4, L4/L5, L5/S1), vertebral bodies (L3-L5), spinal canal (CSF), posterior paraspinal muscles, and vertebral marrow in one FOV.

Structures in FOV: nucleus pulposus (L3/L4, L4/L5, L5/S1), annulus fibrosus (L3/L4, L4/L5, L5/S1), paraspinal muscle (erector spinae), cerebrospinal fluid (spinal canal), vertebral body marrow (L3, L4, L5), spinal cord (conus medullaris / cauda equina), subcutaneous fat (posterior)

Differential analysis plan:

  • ROI-averaged Z-spectra are computed per offset. MTRasym(3.5 ppm) = Z(-3.5) - Z(+3.5) is the primary metric. For GAG confirmation, we expect: nucleus pulposus >> annulus fibrosus > paraspinal muscle ≈ CSF ≈ vertebral marrow in MTRasym(3.5). A Lorentzian fit at 3.5 ppm (Gaussian-line amide pool) across ROIs should yield amplitudes that correlate with known GAG concentrations (NP:AF:muscle ~ 100:75:5).
  • The negative offset (-3.5 ppm) pool (aliphatic rNOE) should show the opposite pattern (higher in marrow and muscle due to lipid content). If MTRasym(3.5) differences track GAG concentration, this confirms GAG-specific CEST. If all ROIs show similar MTRasym(3.5) despite 20× concentration differences, the effect is non-specific background MT/NOE.

Not actively targeted: Lactate, Sodium ion (Na+), and Chloride ion (Cl-) were excluded as they showed low/no simulated CEST contrast at any field strength in the physicist's analysis. These would not produce detectable Z-spectrum signals under our protocol conditions and are not worth the additional scan time.

Caveats:

  • Partial-voluming: lumbar discs are thin (~8-12 mm), so NP and AF ROIs may mix near their border. B0 inhomogeneity from adjacent bone/disc interfaces can shift Z-spectra despite WASSR correction. B1 inhomogeneity from body coil transmission (±30% across the lumbar spine FOV) will differentially affect saturation efficiency across ROIs.
  • The compromise B1=0.8 µT, Tsat=1000 ms favours the 3.5 ppm amide but may undersaturate fast-exchanging hydroxyls at 0.8 ppm. Susceptibility from bowel gas anteriorly and bone posteriorly may degrade field homogeneity. One metabolite (GAG) makes the compromise choice straightforward, but the single B1/Tsat limits detection of any exchange regime mismatch.
